name: Ajwain
note: Thyme-like and aggressive. A quarter teaspoon changes a whole pan of potatoes.

name: Allspice
note: Clove, nutmeg and pepper from one berry. Enough on its own to carry a jerk rub.

name: Anise seed
note: Sweeter and softer than star anise, and about half as loud.

name: Annatto
note: More colour than flavour. Steep it in warm fat and the fat turns orange in a minute.

name: Black cardamom
note: Smoked over a fire. Camphor and campfire, not perfume. Don't swap it for green cardamom.

name: Brown mustard seed
note: Pop it in hot oil and it turns nutty. Ground into a cold paste it stays sharp.

name: Caraway
note: Rye bread, to most people. A pinch sharpens a paprika-heavy blend.

name: Celery seed
note: Small, bitter and very strong.

name: Coriander seed
note: Citrus-warm and forgiving. Grinds husky, so sieve it if you want a smooth curry.

name: Cumin
note: The workhorse. Toast it — untoasted it tastes flat.

name: Dill seed
note: Sharper and more bitter than the leaf. Better in a pickling brine than a dry rub.

name: Fennel seed
note: Sweet anise. Good with pork, tomato and cabbage. Loses its top note fast once ground.

name: Fenugreek seed
note: Maple and bitterness, the note behind shop-bought curry powder. Don't over-toast it.

name: Grains of paradise
note: Peppery heat with cardamom behind it. Use it instead of black pepper in a finishing blend.

name: Green cardamom
note: Buy pods, not powder. Ground cardamom fades faster than anything else on the shelf.

name: Juniper berry
note: Pine and gin. Crush it rather than mill it.

name: Korarima
note: Ethiopian cardamom. Bigger and smokier than the green pod, and the note you taste first in berbere.

name: Nigella
note: Onion and oregano with a faint bitterness. Goes on bread whole, never ground.

name: Nutmeg
note: Grate it from whole. It takes seconds and the difference is obvious.

name: Poppy seed
note: High in oil and quick to go rancid. Smell it before you use it.

name: Sesame seed
note: Toast it separately and last. It burns while the coriander is still warming up.

name: Star anise
note: One star flavours a whole braise.

name: Yellow mustard seed
note: Milder than brown. The heat only shows up in cold water, and cooking kills it.

name: Cassia
note: What most shops sell as cinnamon. Hotter, sweeter, thick-barked. It will wreck a cheap grinder.

name: Cinnamon (Ceylon)
note: Thin brittle quills, delicate and citrusy where cassia is blunt.

name: Dried ginger
note: A duller, warmer burn than the fresh root. Not a substitute for it.

name: Dried horseradish
note: The heat goes up your nose, not down your throat. Add it off the heat.

name: Galangal
note: Sharper and more medicinal than ginger, with pine behind it. Dried, it loses most of the citrus.

name: Licorice root
note: Sweetens without sugar and rounds off salt. A small piece in a long red-braise.

name: Turmeric
note: Colour and a musty bitterness. Give it a few seconds in hot fat or it tastes chalky.

name: Wasabi powder
note: Most wasabi powder is horseradish, mustard and colouring. Cold water, then leave it ten minutes.

name: Clove
note: The loudest thing here. Past three percent of a blend it flattens everything else.

name: Dried lavender
note: Camphor under the perfume. A heavy hand tastes medicinal. Buy culinary grade.

name: Dried rose petal
note: Turns a heavy warm blend perfumed instead of muddy. Too much and it tastes of soap.

name: Mace
note: The lacy shell around the nutmeg. Same aroma, drier and more bitter, and it won't colour a pale dish.

name: Saffron
note: Steep the threads in warm liquid for ten minutes. Dropped in dry, most of it stays in the thread.

name: Black pepper
note: Buy it whole. Ground pepper is half gone within a month.

name: Cubeb
note: Pepper with pine and a bitter finish.

name: Green peppercorn
note: The unripe berry, freeze-dried. Grassier than black and much less hot.

name: Long pepper
note: Hotter and sweeter than black pepper, with a slow build.

name: Pink peppercorn
note: Not a pepper at all. Fruity, floral, barely hot.

name: Sichuan pepper
note: A tingle rather than heat. Sift out the black seeds first.

name: White pepper
note: The same berry with the skin fermented off. Less aromatic, more directly hot, slightly barnyard.

name: Aleppo pepper
note: Coarse oily flakes with a raisin-and-vinegar edge. Slow heat that never spikes.

name: Ancho
note: Dried poblano. Raisin-sweet and barely hot, the body of most Mexican chile pastes.

name: Bird's eye chili
note: Sharp heat at the front of the mouth, gone quickly. Easy to overshoot.

name: Cayenne
note: Almost pure heat, not much flavour. Use it to raise the burn without changing the taste.

name: Chile de arbol
note: Clean bright heat that holds up in hot oil.

name: Chipotle
note: A jalapeno smoked until leathery. The heat and the smoke arrive together — taste as you go.

name: Gochugaru
note: Sun-dried and coarse, more sweet than hot.

name: Guajillo
note: Tart and berry-like, with a thin skin that grinds cleanly.

name: Kashmiri chili
note: Deep red, and almost no heat.

name: Pasilla
note: Dried chilaca. Darker and more bitter than ancho, with a cocoa edge.

name: Piment d'Espelette
note: Basque, and mild enough to use like pepper.

name: Scotch bonnet
note: Apricot and flowers under serious heat.

name: Smoked paprika
note: Oak-smoked before grinding. A barbecue note for food that never saw fire.

name: Sweet paprika
note: Colour and sweetness rather than heat. It scorches in seconds — stir it into fat off the heat.

name: Urfa biber
note: Sweated in the sun until nearly black. Raisin and dark chocolate.

name: Basil
note: Loses most of itself in drying.

name: Bay leaf
note: Needs liquid and time. Grind it if you want it in a dry rub.

name: Curry leaf
note: Nothing to do with curry powder. Fry it in hot fat until it crackles, about ten seconds.

name: Dill weed
note: Softer and greener than the seed.

name: Dried cilantro
note: A shadow of the fresh leaf, and the first herb here to go dusty. Buy the smallest jar.

name: Dried lemongrass
note: Woody and fibrous once dried. Grind it fine or steep it long.

name: Fenugreek leaf
note: Crush it over a finished curry. That savoury bitterness is the restaurant note.

name: Makrut lime leaf
note: The strongest citrus in a dry pantry. Tear it for soup, shred it fine for anything you eat.

name: Marjoram
note: Sweeter and more floral than oregano.

name: Mexican oregano
note: A different plant from Mediterranean oregano. More citrus, less pine.

name: Oregano
note: Better dried than fresh. Crush it between your palms as it goes in.

name: Parsley
note: Mostly colour once dried.

name: Rosemary
note: Needle-hard even dried. Grind it or you'll find splinters. Dominant past a small pinch.

name: Sage
note: Musty and a little camphorous, built for pork and fat. Rubbed sage is fluffy — weigh it.

name: Spearmint
note: Cooling. Good against a heavy lamb or chilli blend.

name: Summer savory
note: Peppery thyme. It's what makes a Provencal blend taste southern rather than Italian.

name: Tarragon
note: Anise in leaf form, and assertive.

name: Thyme
note: Holds up to long cooking better than any other leaf here.

name: Garlic powder
note: Granulated keeps better than fine powder, which cakes. Keep it out of the toasting pan.

name: Onion powder
note: Sweeter and less sharp than garlic powder.

name: Almond
note: Ground nuts thicken as well as flavour.

name: Amchoor
note: Dried green mango. Sourness without any liquid.

name: Asafoetida
note: Raw it smells like a gas leak. A few seconds in hot fat and it turns into cooked onion and garlic. A pinch is a full dose.

name: Black salt
note: Sulphurous and faintly eggy. The savoury tang in a chaat blend.

name: Brown sugar
note: There to caramelise, not to sweeten. Keep the heat low — it burns fast.

name: Dried lime
note: Fermented and sun-dried. Sour and musty at once. Pierce it whole for a stew, grind it for a rub.

name: Dried orange peel
note: Aged peel loses its sharpness and turns resinous and bitter. Ties warm blends to sour ones.

name: Fine sea salt
note: Weigh it. Salt crystals differ by a factor of two in volume.

name: Hazelnut
note: Toast it and rub the skins off before grinding. Pulse it coarse so it stays crunchy.

name: Sumac
note: Tart and slightly fruity, and it stains everything red. Add it off the heat.

name: Tamarind powder
note: Sour with a dried-fruit depth lemon doesn't have. The powder goes straight into a dry blend.

name: Unsweetened cocoa
note: A little adds bitterness and colour without tasting of chocolate.

name: Vanilla
note: Reads as sweet even with no sugar in the dish.
